answer.text: Rain tapped the window of the bus. Leo checked his watch for the fifth time, tapping his foot on the wet floor. On his knees lay the folder with his drawings, and his hands would not stay still. The driver hummed a cheerful song, which made everything worse. Off the bus he jumped, and up the stairs he ran. Silence in the corridor. A closed door. He had missed the interview by ten minutes, and he had practised his speech for a week. Then a woman appeared at the end of the hall, holding a cup of tea. "Are you Leo?" she asked. "We had to postpone everything. The director, of course, is stuck in traffic." Leo laughed so loudly that the secretary looked up. She offered him a cup of tea, and he drank it slowly. In the end, he got the job. The director arrived an hour later, blaming the bus.

Every Sunday my grandfather used to fish at the lake, and every Sunday he came home with an empty bucket and a happy face. My mother would laugh and say that fishing was only an excuse to sit in silence. One morning I followed him. Into the water went his line, and out of the silence came nothing. Hours passed, and the lake stayed as silent as a painting. Then a tiny silver fish jumped into the bucket by itself. My grandfather stared at it. "Unbelievable," he whispered. His hands shook a little as he held the bucket. I had never seen him so excited, or so suspicious. "Of course," he said at last, "the day I bring a friend, the fish behave." In the end, he let the fish go and told everybody it was the best catch of his life. Since then, he has never fished alone.

answer.text: I would like to put forward a proposal for the open day: a story workshop in the square. Last year, the square had been empty for months, and many neighbours told me they missed a place to meet. A workshop with a small book stall could change that. The square belongs to all of us, and a story is the cheapest way to fill it. I understand that the budget is small, and much as I appreciate your concern, I believe we can manage. I was wondering whether the volunteers could bring the books and the chairs, so the cost would be almost nothing, and nobody would need to spend money on anything else. Should it rain, we will move the workshop into the hall. Failing that, we can shorten the morning. If everyone agrees, I will confirm the stall by Friday, and by Saturday we will have prepared the posters. Shall we agree on that? Thank you for listening, and I hope you will join us.

Let me put forward a proposal: a story workshop for the open day. When I was a child, the square used to be full of people, and I would love to see that again. Stories can bring neighbours together, and a simple workshop is a good way to start. Nobody needs a big stage to tell a story, only a few chairs and a little time. Fair enough, the budget is limited. Much as I would like a bigger stall, I am sure the volunteers can help, and I was wondering whether the library could lend us some books for the morning. In the event of rain, the workshop will take place in the hall. By Friday I will have confirmed the stall with the council, and the posters will be ready by Saturday. That is our deadline, and I am confident that we can meet it together. Are we all happy with this plan?
